newsitem.title: MEXICO: Primary Cetes rates fall on cheery economic news.
newsitem.headline: Primary Cetes rates fall on cheery economic news.

text.p: Interest rates in Mexico's weekly primary auction of treasury bills (Cetes) reversed a three-week trend and fell on Tuesday, largely because of news Mexico would prepay $6 billion in floating-rate bank notes and positive industrial production data, analysts said.
Both jolts of good news hit before bids were placed on Tuesday, leading to a fall of 39 basis points in the benchmark 28-day Cetes to 20.04 percent.
Rates on longer-term paper also fell across the board.
A Reuters survey of nine Cetes dealers forecast a more modest fall of 12 basis points on the one-month paper with three of the participants predicting higher rates.

"I think today was a very special day because of the news on the prepayment and moreover the figures on industrial production," Hector Chavez, an analyst with Santander Investments in Mexico City, told Reuters. "This had a very positive impact."
Mexico's Finance Ministry announced a huge refinancing, largely through bridge loans, to prepay $6 billion in floating-rate bank notes.

Earlier Tuesday, the Finance Ministry said overall industrial activity grew 15.0 percent in April compared to the same month last year, which was nearly twice as high as the 7.92 percent rise predicted in a Reuters survey.

Ricardo Vazquez, an analyst with Banco Union Mexico City, said rates also took a dip on the generally cheaper cost of money recently combined with declining inflation and growing expectations that the Fed will leave U.S. rates intact during the next Open Market Committee meeting in July.
"Since last week we've seen the cost of money (in the secondary market) come back down and that's why we're seeing primary rates down this week," Vazquez told Reuters.
Still, analysts said there are signs of caution in the market, such as a fall in demand to 12.3 billion pesos worth of Cetes this week compared to 13.6 billion pesos last week.

That caution is widely attributed to the July 6 mid-term elections, in which Mexicans will elect all 500 members of the lower house of Congress, one-fourth of the Senate, six state governors and a mayor for Mexico City.

"Until the elections we are going to see short-term rates very volatile between 20 and 21.5 percent," Chavez said. "It's nothing more than nervousness over the elections. In large part the expected (election) results have been taken into account. The fundamental factors (such as key economic indicators) look very good and are calming investors."

Chavez said investors are prepared for the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) to lose much of its advantage in Congress, possibly losing its long-held majority, with the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) taking the mayorship of Mexico City.
One analyst who asked not to be identified said U.S. CPI figures released on Tuesday -- numbers that continue to show U.S. inflation under control -- added to the good Mexican news.

"In addition, these (auction) results reflect greater liquidity in the secondary market tied to the availability of investment dollars by foreigners, which in turn stabilizes the exchange rate," the analyst said.
The Mexican peso has held very steady against the dollar in recent months, so much so that some analysts are concerned about a possible post-election crash.
